key_insight: In these medical foundation models, self-supervised pretraining—not clinical supervision or model scale—was the main driver of representational convergence.
clinical_relevance: A simple linear classifier could transfer across encoders and to five unseen hospitals, suggesting useful interoperability, but the shared representation still falls short of clinical similarity and radiologist judgment.
method: Compared 18 image encoders and 7 text encoders across five imaging modalities
Controlled training to vary only the pretraining objective while holding data, architecture, and scale fixed
Tested alignment on large chest radiography datasets and a synthetic model
evidence_signal: Across 650,982 chest radiographs from six datasets, matched self-supervised encoders aligned most (40.4%), versus 21.1% for label-supervised and 3.3% for image-text models.
watch_item: Convergence was modest, did not increase with size, and may be weakest across patient subgroups or where clinical judgment matters most.
paper_title: Self-supervision drives representational convergence in medical foundation models more than clinical supervision
